GOVERNMENT BILL 
The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (Amendment)  
Bill, 2008 
 THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DE PARTMENT OF COMMER CE, MINISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY AND THE MINISTER  OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): Sir, I move: 
That the Bill to amend the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development 
Authority Act, 1985, as passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration.  
 Sir, with your permission, I would like to ma ke a brief opening statem ent on this important 
Bill that was passed by the Lok Sabha in the last Session and that is coming before this House 
for passage today. 
 Sir, as the hon. Members are aware, Basm ati rice is one of the most well-known and 
internationally recognized geographic indications that comes from this sub-continent. Sir, in 
1999, Parliament passed the Geographical Indication s Registration and Protection Act, and this 
Act came into being in September, 2003. Since then, 104 geographic indications have been 
awarded and are being used in the market place by various users. The first geographic indication 
that was awarded was in 2003 and that was to Darjeeling tea. The present Bill empowers APEDA 
to go for registration of Basmati rice as a geographic indication. 
 Sir, as the hon. Members are aware, in the last few years, there have been a number of 
instances where the name Basmati has been infringed upon in various parts of the world. In the 
U.S. itself, there have been a number of case s where Basmati rice is being sold under the 
trademark of Texmati, Canmati and so on and so forth. In fact, Sir, we have documented over 
300 instances where the name Basmati has been wrongly used. What this Bill does is it 
empowers APEDA to go for a geograp hic indication so that the name  Basmati is fully protected. 
Basmati, of course, is the first and most promin ent example of the benefit that will accrue from 
this Bill.  
 There are many other instances where intellectua l property rights on food products can be 
protected, both in India as well as abroad. Sir, in  India, the word ‘Basmati’ is used for aromatic 
rice, long-grain rice that is cu ltivated predominantly in Punjab , Haryana, Uttarakhand, Western 
U.P. and parts of Jammu and Kashmir. Today, anywhere between 3-4 lakh farmers grow 
Basmati rice  and, this year i.e., 2008-09, we estima te that about 1.5-1.6 million tonnes of 
Basmati rice would be exported and the total export earnings would be anywhere between Rs. 
7,000-7,500 crores. Now, the traditional rights of the farmers are not being impinged upon in 
any way through this proposed legislation. All that  this legislation does is to empower APEDA to 
own the Trade Mark or Geographic Indication of Ba smati for the benefit of the users and fight for 
the infringement of the word Basmati. 

 4
 On 28th November, 2008, APEDA has already applied to the Geographic Indications 
Registry which is located in Chennai. This whole process takes about 6-7 months, and we hope 
that at the end of this period the Geographic In dication for Basmati rice would be given. The 
owner of the Geographic Indication would be APEDA like the Tea Board is the owner for the 
Geographic Indications of Darjeeling Tea. Like wise, the APEDA would then be empowered by 
Parliament to have the statutory powers to fight for protection of Basmati. 
 Sir, I will just make one more point before I conclude. This is with regard to joint registration 
of Basmati rice with Pakistan. It is a very important issue. As you know, Sir, traditionally, 
Basmati rice has been an appellation of rice not only grown in India but also in Pakistan. Basmati 
rice belongs to the Himalayan foothills of the undivided subcontinent. We have had a large 
number of meetings with Pakistan over the last few years. The last meeting of the Joint Working 
Group on Basmati rice was held on 7-8th Nove mber, 2008. Our intention was to go and explore 
the possibility of a joint Geographic Indication, particularly in the E.U., because we export about 
1.5 million tonnes of Basmati rice and Pakistan exports about 1.2 million tonnes of Basmati rice. 
Sir, Basmati is important for India and Pakistan  and nowhere else in the world it is grown. 
Unfortunately, because of the horrendous attacks on 26th November in Mumbai, all negotiations 
and communications on this issue have been put on the backburner and rightly so. We had 
arrived at some way forward of joint action with Pa kistan. But, I am afraid, that will have to wait 
till full normalisation of relations take place. Mean while, Sir, what has happened — this is what 
gives urgency to this Bill today — is that a body called the Basmati Growers Association in 
Lahore applied and got the Trade Mark on the word Basmati from the Registrar of Trade Marks 
in Pakistan. The APEDA has objected to it. Those objections have not been taken into 
consideration and the Trade Mark ‘Basmati’ was given. Sir, APEDA’s case was weak, because 
there was no statutory backing for APEDA for owning this Geographic Indication. Now, the 
appeal of APEDA against this decision of the Paki stani Registrar of Trade Mark in the High Court 
of Sindh in Karachi has been admitted and we hope that this appeal will be heard and APEDA’s 
appeal will result in trade mark been given to the Basmati Growers Association of Lahore will be 
nullified and, with the statutory backing that the APEDA will have, we believe, this would 
enormously strengthen APEDA’s case. After APEDA gets the Geographic Indication in India, we 
will apply for Geographic Indication in Europe, because we cannot apply for protection abroad 
unless we protect the name in our own country. I am sorry that it has really taken us so long. It is 
something that this should have happened many  years ago. But, unfortunately, because of a 
variety of reasons, we have not been able to protect the word Basmati which, in my view,  
should have been done immediately after the Act was passed by Parliament in 1999 and notified 
in 2003. 

 5
 Sir, the word ‘basmati’, I reiterate is used for long range aromatic rice grown in Punjab, 
Haryana, Uttarakhand, Western U.P. and parts of Jammu & Kashmir. I say this, Sir, because 
there is a great move, there is a demand, there is a desire to expand the definition of what is 
basmati rice. Today, rice grown in Madhya Prad esh, rice grown in Kerala, rice grown in 
Karnataka is being claimed as basmati rice. Sir, this makes a mockery of the word ‘basmati’. I 
appeal to the hon. Members of the House that le t us restrict basmati to  the Himalayan foothills 
and not define basmati in such a general way that  it makes the protection totally meaningless. I 
say this, Sir, because I have got requests from  various Members of Parliament belonging to 
some different States saying that their rice shou ld also be classified as basmati rice. I make a 
humble plea to all such Members not to expand th e definition of basmati to make it completely 
meaningless; otherwise, we will not be able to provide protection for this word ‘basmati rice’. 
 With these few words, Sir, I commend this Bill to the House. 
The question was proposed.
